title: Number of Islands
statement:
You're given a 2D grid `grid` whose cells are the strings "1" (land) and "0" (water). An island is a group of land cells connected horizontally or vertically; cells that only touch diagonally are not connected. Return the number of islands.

The grid may be empty, in which case there are no islands. Treat everything outside the grid as water.

Constraints: 0 <= rows <= 100; 1 <= columns <= 100 when there is at least one row; every cell is exactly the string "1" or "0".

examples.explanation: The top-left group, the group in the middle right, and the lone cell in the corner. The corner cell only touches the middle group diagonally.
No two land cells share a side, so each of the five is its own island.
The land forms a single ring around a one-cell lake.

hints: Pick one land cell. Which other cells belong to the same island, and how would you find all of them?
Once you have found a whole island, how do you make sure you never count any of its cells again?
Walk through the grid cell by cell. What should happen when you meet land that you haven't seen yet, and when you meet land you have?
Check the grid [[1,0],[0,1]]: should the two cells join up? Also think about what happens at the edges of the grid.
Scan every cell; each time you find unvisited land, count one island and flood-fill it (DFS or BFS) while marking cells visited.
followUps: What are the time and space complexity, and what input makes your extra space largest?
Your solution changes the grid as it goes. What would you do if the input must not be modified?
If you used recursive DFS, what could go wrong on a large snake-shaped island, and how would you avoid it?
What if the land cells arrive one at a time and you must report the island count after each one?
How would you change the code to also report the area of the largest island, or to treat diagonal neighbours as connected?
idealAnswerPoints: Counts connected components of land cells under 4-directional adjacency
Scans every cell and starts a flood fill (DFS or BFS) only from unvisited land
Marks cells as visited, either in a separate set or by sinking them in the grid
Checks the grid bounds before looking at a neighbour, and handles an empty grid
States O(rows * cols) time and explains the space cost of the stack, queue or visited set
weakAnswerSigns: Counts every land cell, or every land cell whose neighbour is water, instead of components
Forgets to mark visited cells and recurses forever or double-counts
Compares cells with the integer 1 instead of the string "1"

rubric.correctness: Right island count on every test, including an empty grid, all water, all land, diagonal-only contacts, rings and lakes.
rubric.efficiency: Each cell is visited a constant number of times: O(rows * cols). Re-scanning the grid per island is too slow.
rubric.code_quality: Bounds checks in one place, a single clear visited mechanism and a neat way to enumerate the four neighbours.
rubric.communication: Explains the flood-fill idea and states clearly whether and why the input grid is modified.
